name: Cold desert
notes: Sparse grey chenopod shrubs (saltbush, saxaul, winterfat) and scattered bunchgrasses with cold winters; Gobi and Central Asian deserts, Great Basin/Colorado Plateau lowlands, Patagonian monte.

canopy.name: Fremont cottonwood

traits.native_range: Populus fremontii, SW USA canyon streams, 12-30 m, bright green — USDA PLANTS
traits.leaf_shape: simple or compound broad leaves, most deciduous in cold bands

traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

canopy.silhouette: broad open crown on massive pale trunk, yellow autumn

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds germinate within 24-48 h on wet, bare sand left by receding spring floods, and the tiny seedling's root must keep pace with the falling water table (4-13 mm a day). Survivors form dense, even-aged bands of slender whips along the channel, with shiny, broadly triangular, coarsely toothed leaves on flattened stalks that turn gold in autumn.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Populus fremontii (germinates within 24-48 h; seed viable 1-5 weeks, lost if not in a wet microsite in 2-3 days; seedling roots grow 4-12 mm a day; reproductive at 5-10 yr; 6-34 m tall; lives more than 130 yr; wind pollinated). Height-growth years estimated from riparian cottonwood growth rates.

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS Populus fremontii (flowers early spring, done by end of May; male catkins 3.8-8.3 cm, female 10-12.7 cm; seed shed Feb-June by region; entirely wind pollinated). Capsule size, days to ripen and crop follow P. deltoides (USDA Silvics); colour is the red male catkins.

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds germinate within hours of wetting (the embryo is a ready-made, coiled green seedling) and emerge in 1-3 days: tiny green shoots with two slender cotyledons, then jointed, leafless green twigs. Deep roots race down; young plants are small feathery shrubs of drooping green twigs that later thicken into a gnarled, grey, twisted trunk.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Haloxylon ammodendron: 2-8 m, rarely 12 m; trunk to 25 cm); saxaul literature (very rapid germination, green spirally coiled embryo, short seed viability). Growth and ages estimated.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (tiny flowers Mar-Apr; fruit winged by the spreading perianth, ~8 mm across, pale brown or white wings, ripe Oct-Nov; seed 1.5 mm). Wind pollination, timings and counts estimated from shrubby Amaranthaceae.

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings, usually from seeds cached by jays under shrubs, have 7-9 cotyledons and bluish primary needles, then unique single, round, stiff, sharp grey-green needles (the only pine with one needle per bundle). Young trees are compact, bluish cones; old ones become rounded, flat-topped and often multi-stemmed.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Pinus monophylla: a dominant tree takes ~60 years to reach 2 m and ~150 to reach 8.5 m (about 5 cm/yr); first cones ~35 yrs, good crops from 75-100, peak at 160-200; not shade tolerant; dominants often 400 years, some 800-1,000

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS (strobili late spring-early summer, pollen shed by mid-June; three-season cone cycle, ripe seed about 26 months after the buds form; cones 3.5-5.5 cm, thick-scaled, open Sep-Nov; masting every 2-3 years); its large wingless nuts were a Great Basin staple

canopy.silhouette: squat multi-trunk juniper, half dead limbs, rounded crown

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings have needle-like juvenile leaves 5-10 mm long, making a soft, prickly little blue-green cone; scale leaves take over within a few years. Growth is very slow (often only a few cm a year) and seedlings usually establish under a nurse shrub, becoming after decades a rounded, bushy, often multi-trunked tree with shreddy grey bark.
growth.source: USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual (J. osteosperma: flowers Mar-Apr, cones ripen in 2nd year, reddish-brown with bloom, persist ~2 yr, 1-2 seeds, good crops about every 2 yr, bears from 10-20 yr); Wikipedia (3-6 m, cones 8-13 mm maturing in ~18 months, juvenile needles 5-10 mm). Growth rate and longevity estimated.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (cones 8-13 mm, blue-brown with whitish waxy bloom, mature in ~18 months, pollen shed early spring; eaten and dispersed by jackrabbits, coyotes, solitaires); USDA WPSM (reddish-brown ripe cones persist ~2 yr). Set, crop and rot estimated.

shrub.name: American winterfat

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two narrow woolly cotyledons, then narrow grey-green leaves thick with white star-shaped hairs. Seed germinates in near-freezing soil in early spring; the young plant is a small silver-grey woolly sprig over a deep taproot, branching from a woody base into a low twiggy subshrub that turns white with fluffy fruits in autumn.
growth.source: USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual, Krascheninnikovia lanata (20-80 cm; flowers Jun-Aug; wind-pollinated; hairy-bracted fruits shed fall-winter; may seed in its first year; germinates at near-freezing temperatures). Lifespan estimated.

repro.note: wind-pollinated, mostly monoecious; the white-haired fruits blow across the snow in winter

shrub.source: Krascheninnikovia lanata (syn. Ceratoides lanata, Eurotia lanata), salt-desert shrubland, sagebrush steppe and cold plains from Saskatchewan to northern Mexico, woolly subshrub 1-8 dm — Flora of North America vol. 4; USDA FEIS; Kew POWO for the accepted name (the Eurasian K. ceratoides is a separate species).

traits.native_range: Salt-desert shrubland and cold plains of western North America

traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

bark.notes: young twigs white-woolly; the woody base grey-brown and shreddy

flower.form: tiny greyish flowers in dense leafy spikes at the stem tips

fruit.form: fruit enclosed in two bracts tufted with long silky white hairs 4-8 mm; whole stem tips look like white wool

shrub.name: Big sagebrush
shrub.source: Artemisia tridentata, dominant Great Basin shrub, grey-green aromatic 0.6-2.5 m — USDA PLANTS

traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: two small round cotyledons, then narrow, entire, silvery-hairy leaves; the wedge-shaped leaves with three blunt teeth at the tip come a few weeks later. It stays a single-stemmed silver sprig for a year or two while its roots race down, then branches into a rounded, aromatic, silver-grey bush with a short twisted trunk and shreddy bark.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Artemisia tridentata subsp. tridentata: germination in 2-3 days at all test temperatures, in late fall/winter or after snowmelt; plants 2-3 yr old can bear viable seed; commonly 40-50 yr, some over 100 yr; 1-2 m, up to 5 m. Height-age curve and shade class estimated.

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS basin big sagebrush: flowers late Aug-Oct; seed ripens and disperses Oct-Dec over ~8 weeks, ~90% within 9 m; self- or wind-pollinated; more prolific than Wyoming big sagebrush. Tiny heads of a few florets in leafy panicles; fruit set and crop estimated.

shrub.name: Blackbrush

traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings usually come up in clumps from forgotten rodent seed caches: tiny epigeal seedlings with two oval cotyledons and small narrow opposite leaves; most die at the cotyledon stage. Survivors grow very slowly into a dense, rounded, rigidly branched grey shrub whose twigs end in spines and turn blackish when wet, hence the name.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Coleogyne ramosissima (slow-growing shrub 0.3-1.8 m on shallow soils, long-lived, flowers in spring from buds formed ~2 wk after March growth, apetalous solitary terminal flowers, wind-pollinated, achenes 3-4 mm, a masting species, rodent caches give clumped seedlings, 53-83% germination with 7 wk stratification, most seedlings die); ages estimated

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS Coleogyne ramosissima (solitary terminal flowers with 4 yellowish petal-like sepals and no petals, spring only; wind pollination; dry leathery achenes 3-4 mm with a twisted style, ripe early summer; mast years with huge crops, scatter-hoarded by rodents)

traits.native_range: Atriplex confertifolia, Great Basin saline valley floors, spiny grey shrub 0

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds need a winter of chilling and sprout in spring. Epigeal seedling with two narrow cotyledons and small, round-oval, grey scurfy leaves; it grows slowly into a compact, rounded, grey-green shrublet whose older twigs harden into short spines. Seedlings survive best beside an established shrub.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Atriplex confertifolia (chilling needed, fungal breakdown of bracteoles, relatively short-lived, seedlings survive best near adults); Woody Plant Seed Manual (rarely germinable without chilling); growth rate and ages estimated.

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS (flowers late Mar-mid Jun, dioecious, wind-pollinated, utricles in 2 round bracts 4-12 mm, mature ~25 weeks after flowering, persist through winter); Woody Plant Seed Manual (65-277 thousand fruits/kg); PFAF (seed eaten as mush); crop estimated.

ground.name: Desert crust moss
ground.origin: Dry lands of the N Hemisphere

growth.juvenile_note: Mostly starts from a broken shoot fragment blown onto bare soil between shrubs; it buds tiny upright shoots a few mm tall that crowd into low dark cushions. Dry, the leaves twist tight and the patch looks black-brown, frosted by the white hair-points; within minutes of rain they spread open bright green.
growth.source: Flora of North America vol. 27, Syntrichia caninervis (shoots to about 1 cm; leaves with a long hyaline awn; on soil in arid regions; sporophytes rare). Ages and spread estimated from soil-crust moss studies.

repro.note: spores by wind and water and, far more often, broken shoot fragments; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.source: Syntrichia caninervis, the dominant moss of the biological soil crusts of the Great Basin, Mojave, Colorado Plateau and the Central Asian deserts (Gurbantunggut, Gobi), on soil between and under shrubs — Flora of North America vol. 27 (Pottiaceae); Tropicos for the name.

appearance.silhouette: dark speckled patches on bare soil between shrubs
appearance.refs: Flora of North America vol. 27; Belnap & Lange, Biological Soil Crusts

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings emerge with the summer rains (June-July) as a thin tuft of narrow grey-green blades; roots reach about 25 cm in 6 weeks. From the second year scaly rhizomes 2.5-5 cm deep creep out (up to 1.5-1.8 m) and send up new tufts, so the plant becomes a patchy sod of stiff, curly-bladed culms 20-50 cm tall topped by compact spikes 3-7 cm long.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Pleuraphis jamesii (85% germination at 15.5-32 C; seedling roots 24.7 cm at 6 weeks; emergence June-July; rhizomes 1.5-1.8 m long, persist 5-7+ yr; resprouts regain preburn cover within 2 yr; culms 8-61 cm; spikes 3-7 cm). Age at first seed and plant lifespan estimated.

The seedling is a single thin tiller with rolled, wiry, blue-green leaves above a fast, deep root; it slowly tillers into a small dense bunch and usually flowers from its second year, with airy, open panicles of plump black seeds on zigzag stalks.

Index Fungorum for the name; Gilbertson & Ryvarden, North American Polypores.

Bunches enlarge by new crown tillers (each tiller lives about two seasons) into a fine, fountain-like tussock that sends up spikes of long, curly-awned 'needle and thread' seeds in early summer.
growth.source: NDSU autecology of needle and thread (tillers live two growing seasons, regeneration mainly by crown tillers, low seedling success, flowers late May-June); USDA NRCS Plant Guide (seed dormancy, slow establishment, flowers June, seed July); germination, growth and lifespan values estimated.

ground.name: Rock shield lichen

growth.juvenile_note: Starts as a few millimetre lobes of yellow-green thallus on sunny rock or bare soil, spreading outward a few mm a year into a loose round rosette of narrow, branching, flat lobes with a black underside; old rosettes die in the centre and break into rings.
growth.source: Brodo, Sharnoff & Sharnoff 2001 Lichens of North America (Xanthoparmelia: foliose rosettes on rock and soil, yellow-green, lower surface black or brown). Growth rate and ages estimated from other foliose rock lichens.

repro.note: a lichen: fungal spores and broken lobes or isidia by wind and water; no flowers; grows only while wet

ground.source: Xanthoparmelia coloradoensis, a loosely attached yellow-green foliose lichen on rocks and soil of the Great Plains, Rocky Mountains and the Great Basin and Colorado Plateau — Hale 1990 synopsis of Xanthoparmelia (Smithsonian Contributions to Botany 74); Index Fungorum for the name.

ground.name: Squirreltail

growth.juvenile_note: Germinates in autumn or early spring as a single thin tiller of flat or rolled grey-green blades; it tillers into a small, tight bunch and from the second season sends up stiff culms with bristly spikes whose long purplish awns spread like a bottle brush, breaking apart at maturity and tumbling with the wind.
growth.source: Flora of North America vol. 24 (Elymus elymoides: culms 10-60 cm, cespitose; spikes 3-15 cm, disarticulating at the rachis; awns 2-10 cm, spreading). Germination, first seed and lifespan estimated from cool-season bunchgrass biology.

repro.note: largely self-pollinated; the ripe spike breaks into awned pieces that tumble in the wind and catch in fur

ground.source: Elymus elymoides (syn. Sitanion hystrix), a short-lived native bunchgrass of salt-desert shrubland, sagebrush and pinyon-juniper across the Great Basin and Colorado Plateau, 10-60 cm — Flora of North America vol. 24; USDA FEIS; Kew POWO for the name.
